hints: The answer must be strictly greater than n, even when n itself is prime.
Test odd candidates after n; every composite number has a divisor no larger than its square root.
With n up to 10^12, use a deterministic 64-bit primality test such as Miller-Rabin rather than trial division.
analogy: A composite candidate can be exposed by a witness that proves it is not prime.
example: After 42, candidate 43 is prime, so the next prime is 43.
algorithm: For each candidate n+1,n+2,..., test primality with deterministic Miller-Rabin bases valid for 64-bit integers; skip even values after checking 2. Use overflow-safe modular multiplication.
correctness: Miller-Rabin's chosen deterministic bases distinguish every composite in the supported integer range; checking candidates in order ensures the first prime found is the next one.
complexity: O(g log N) modular multiplications for gap g, with O(1) extra space.
